root.text:
So. You have been looking at my building.

Not living in it — *looking* at it. There is a difference and I have been in this trade long enough to hear it through a floor. A man who lives in a building walks the same line to his door every night and never once counts the steps. A man who is looking at it stops on the landing.

You have stopped on the landing four times this week, Oliver. Come in. Mind the corridor, it is longer today than it was contracted to be.

options.text: "The corridor is longer when I walk it alone."
"Somebody in this building types at night."
"Landy's repair notices are all stamped by the Coalition."
"Say that again. All of it. I want to hear it twice."

check.success_text:
You keep your face entirely out of it and let him run the whole explanation again, and you do not help him, and you do not nod, and you do not do the small encouraging noise that a listener makes without knowing they are making it.

The second telling is nine words shorter. One of the nine is 'contracted'.

He notices that you noticed. He stops halfway through a sentence, looks at you for a moment with something that is not quite offence, and then decides in your favour.

"Mm," he says. "Yes. It goes down each time and I have never had it go down in front of a witness before." And he pours you something, from a bottle that lives behind the charts, and does not offer an explanation of the bottle either.
check.failure_text:
He gets four sentences in — and they are good sentences, they are going somewhere, the charts are already coming off the shelf — and then something crosses your face.

He stops. He adjusts. And what you get instead is the version for a man who is having difficulty: warmer, considerably shorter, delivered with a hand on your shoulder, and with nothing whatsoever in it.

clue.title: Nine words shorter
clue.text: Asimov's second telling drops the word 'contracted'. The corridor is longer than it was contracted to be, and a contract has parties.

corridor.text: It is longer when you walk it alone, yes. It is shorter with two. With four it is a formality. This is not mysterious, Oliver, it is *load-bearing* — a corridor exists to be between two places, and betweenness is a service, and a service scales to demand. One man needs more corridor than four men do. One man has further to go.

passive.text:
That made sense.

That made complete, satisfying, structural sense while he was saying it — you followed every step, you would have signed your name to it — and it is already going. Not forgotten: *withdrawn*, actively, the way the blue is being withdrawn from your notebook, and there is nothing left in the place where it was except the memory of having understood something.

options.text: Write it down before it goes.

check.success_text:
You have the notebook out before he has finished, and you get it — in full, in your own hand, every clause, and the writing holds while you write it.

You read it back.

It is nine words long.

It was four minutes long when he said it. You were there. You listened to the whole of it and followed the whole of it and the four minutes were not padding — and the nine words are: *a corridor is a service and services scale down.*

That is not a summary. A summary is something you make. Nobody made this. That is what survived, and the rest did not go into the notebook and did not stay in the room and is not anywhere now.
check.failure_text:
You have the notebook out before he has finished the sentence, and you get the first clause down cleanly.

The second clause is gone by the time the pencil reaches the place it should go. Not forgotten — *gone*, the way a word is gone when the room has decided you did not hear it — and the pencil goes on moving across the page for a while afterwards out of pure politeness, making the shapes of a sentence that is no longer available.

clue.title: Four minutes, nine words
clue.text: Asimov's explanations are true while spoken and compress on the page. Four minutes of structural sense reduces to: 'a corridor is a service and services scale down.'

write_it_ok.text:
You wrote it down. Good. That is more than most manage — most of them get halfway and their hand stops and they look at me as though I have done it to them on purpose.

Now read it to me.

... Yes. That is what I said.

That is the whole of what I said, and I spoke for four minutes, and both of those facts are true at the same time and I have made my peace with living between them. It took some years. There was a period in the eighties where I did not sleep well about it at all.

You have not made your peace with it yet. You will. Everyone in this building does, or moves out, and the ones who move out do not remember why.

options.text: "Who hasn't made their peace with it?"

who_hasnt.text:
Me. I have not, obviously. I said I had made peace; I said it in the tone a man uses when he has made an arrangement and calls it peace to save time.

I was a cartographer, Oliver. Before the nets, before this. A man who draws coastlines learns one thing above all others, and it is this: the coastline is not the length you measure. It is the length you measure *at the scale you chose*. Change the scale, change the coast. There is no true length of Ireland.

I have lived thirty years in a building where somebody keeps changing the scale. And I have never once caught the hand doing it.

lucid.3: He says 'the hand'. Not the cause, not the phenomenon, not the building. The hand.

clue.title: Somebody keeps changing the scale
clue.text: Asimov, a former cartographer: there is no true length of a coastline, only the length at the chosen scale. He has spent thirty years in a building where somebody changes the scale, and has never caught the hand.

hand.text:
I said 'the hand'. Yes. I have said it that way for years and I have never examined why, and I would rather you did not make me start at my age.

— No. That is cowardice, and you came in here with wet shoes and a question, so. Here is what I have and it is not much: whatever adjusts this building does it the way a *man* does it. Not the way weather does it. It corrects. It goes back over. Twice I have found the same repair made twice, differently, as though somebody had reconsidered.

And once — once, Oliver, and I have told nobody — I found it made three times, and the third one was worse than the first, and it had been put back to the first.

clue.title: Made twice, differently. Once, three times.
clue.text: Asimov has found the same repair made twice in different ways, as though reconsidered — and once made three times, the third worse, and put back to the first.

typing.text:
Ah. The typing.

Yes. Every resident hears it. Every resident, at every hour, on every floor — I have had it raised with me eleven times in nine years and I have raised it with myself considerably more often than that.

No resident owns a machine. I want to be exact about how I know: I have keys to every flat in this building and I have been into every one of them and I have looked. Not glanced — looked, in cupboards, under beds, in the places a man puts a thing he does not want found.

I looked because a manager who does not look is a landlord. There is no typewriter in the Hang-Hi Quiet Apartments.

options.text: "You looked. That means you thought there might be."

check.success_text:
He does not answer for long enough that the answer is the pause.

"I thought there might be," he says, "because for one week in the spring the sound came from a specific direction, and I stood in the corridor at two in the morning with my hand on a door, and the direction was 2F."

A pause of a different quality.

"2F is your flat, Oliver. You were in the harbour that week. You were in the harbour that week and the flat was empty and the sound was coming from inside it and I did not open the door, and I have had a year to decide whether that was cowardice or courtesy, and I have not decided."
check.failure_text:
"I looked because I look. It is a building; things get into buildings. A man brought a goat up to 3C in the spring and did not think to mention it, and I found out from the carpet."

He turns a chart over, which is what Asimov Sobeleaux does instead of ending a conversation, and which ends the conversation.

clue.title: The sound came from 2F
clue.text: For one week last spring the typing had a direction, and the direction was 2F — Oliver's own flat, empty at the time. Asimov stood outside it and did not open the door.

typing_2f.text:
Do not ask me to go in with you. I will say yes and then I will be busy, and we will both have to live with the shape of that.

But I will tell you the thing I have kept back, since we are here and since you are wet and since I am too old to be careful for both of us. The sound stopped the day you came out of the water.

Not the day the — whatever it was — came down. The day *you* came out. I have the date. I have it in the book because I noted it as the day the building went quiet, and I noted it before I knew you had been pulled out, and the two entries are one line apart.

clue.title: It stopped the day you came out of the water
clue.text: Asimov's book records the building going quiet on the same day Oliver was pulled from the harbour — noted before he knew about the rescue, one line apart.

forms.text:
The Coalition, yes. They stamp. It is what they are for.

Understand me: they do not repair. Landy does not repair either, but Landy at least fails at repairing, which is a form of trying. The Coalition receives the failure and issues a word. The word is RESOLVED. Nothing about the building changes and everything about the *file* does, and the file is what the Coalition lives in.

check.success_text:
"I let them," he agrees, "and here is why, and you will not like it and neither do I.

Before they began stamping, the corridor did not simply vary. It *ended*, sometimes, four feet short of my door, and there was nothing past the end — not a wall, Oliver. Nothing. I put my hand into it once.

They stamped it RESOLVED. It has never ended since. It varies, it stretches, it is impertinent — but it goes all the way to the door every single time.

So yes. I let them. Whatever they are doing with those words, the words are holding something up."
check.failure_text:
"I let them."

He turns a chart over. The accent has gone almost entirely, which happens when the subject is ordinary.

"A man my age chooses what he will be tired about. There is a list and it is not a long one and everything else goes on the other list. I have chosen the boiler."

clue.title: The stamps are holding something up
clue.text: Before the Quad-C began stamping, the corridor sometimes ended four feet short of the door with nothing beyond it. Since RESOLVED, it has always reached the door. Their words are structural.

forms_hold.text:
You have the look, Oliver.

The one you get before a sentence with three subordinate clauses in it — the eyebrow comes down and the head goes very slightly to the left and the whole face becomes an argument that has not been made yet.

Go on. Say the thing.

I have been waiting some years for a tenant to say it to me, so that I do not have to be the man who said it first in his own building.

options.text: "If their words hold the building up, then the building is made of words."

check.success_text:
He does not flinch and he does not agree. He does something worse: he nods, slowly, the way a man nods at an arithmetic he checked long ago.

"Sobeleaux," he says. "You never did ask about the name. As above, so below — my grandmother's joke, and she thought it was about the fishing. Above the water, below the water. The same shape twice.

Oliver. If the building is made of words, then so is the man standing in it telling you so. I have known that for eleven years. It has not once stopped me putting the bins out. I recommend the bins. They are the only argument against it that has ever worked."
check.failure_text:
"Made of words." He weighs it, and sets it down, and turns a chart over. "That is a poem, Oliver, and I have a boiler. Come back when it is a measurement."

The accent has gone flat. It does that when he has decided a conversation is over and would prefer not to say so.

clue.title: As above, so below
clue.text: Asimov has known for eleven years that Silvora Reefs is made of language, and has kept putting the bins out. He recommends the bins.

options.text: Say nothing. Let him keep it.

say_it_ok.text:
Go and see Soliloquy, if you have not. She has a vault she keeps shut and she keeps it shut for a reason, and the reason has your name on it in a hand I recognise and would rather not place.

And Oliver — take the corridor slowly on the way out. It is long tonight. It is long because you are going alone, and you are going alone, and there is no arrangement in this world by which that is not true.

name.text:
Sobeleaux. So-be-low. Yes.

My grandmother's, and she thought it was about fishing — above the water, below the water, the same shape twice and only one of them is yours. She said it at every meal for as long as I knew her and I did not understand it until she was dead, which I am told is the usual arrangement with grandmothers.

Everybody gets there eventually. Most of them get there in the second year.

You got there faster than most, and you have been carrying it about for a week without asking me — which is worse manners and better instinct, and I would rather have the instinct in a tenant than the manners.
